title: Medicine
hookLine: Luke the beloved physician, a Samaritan with oil and wine: Christians see healing by doctors as God's work too

cards: Hospitals carry some telling names. Good Samaritan. Mercy.
Saint Luke's. That last name belongs to a man the New Testament names only in passing. In a greeting at the end of one of Paul's letters, he's called "Luke, the beloved physician."

Tradition says this is the same Luke who wrote a Gospel and the book of Acts. A doctor, standing right in the middle of the early church's story, and nobody in it seems to think that's strange. Today: medicine.

teach.b: Jesus himself reaches for the doctor when he describes his own work. Criticized for eating with sinners, he answers: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick."
He doesn't treat the physician as a rival to God. He uses the physician as the picture. Then there's the Good Samaritan, whose name ended up on hospitals too.
Look at what he actually does on that road.

teach.h: OIL AND WINE ON THE WOUNDS.
teach.b: He "bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine." That's first aid, the medicine of the day. Then he brings the man to an inn, pays, and tells the innkeeper, "Take care of him."
Emergency care, then ongoing care, with the bill covered. One more text, the book of Sirach, sits in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and among the Apocrypha in some Protestant ones.
It tells readers to honor the physician, because the Lord created him, and it says the Lord brings medicines out of the earth. Put these together and you get a way of seeing medicine.
When someone gets well under a surgeon's hands or a nurse's patience or a pharmacist's careful counting, Christians who see it this way don't call it God's work or the doctor's. They call it both.
God heals, and very often God heals through hands. That's why prayer and medicine are allowed to sit in the same room.

how: Christians pray for the sick and for those who treat them; churches run hospitals, clinics and nursing ministries, and some keep a feast of Saint Luke, when they remember doctors and pray for healers.

games.q: you're the Samaritan. you've bandaged the stranger's wounds by the road. he still can't walk, and you have business to get to. what do you do?
o: leave him by the road, better than you found him.
carry him to an inn and pay for his care.
hurry on and send someone back later.
games.why: he takes him to an inn, pays, and tells the innkeeper, "Take care of him": emergency care, then ongoing care, with the bill covered.

practice: Bring to mind one time someone helped you, or someone you love, get well: a doctor who explained things slowly, a nurse on a night shift, a pharmacist who caught a mistake, a parent with a bandage and a steady voice.
Let one face come clear, and remember what their hands actually did. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for that person by name; if you don't, just let yourself be grateful to them.

wordCard.voice: Medicine. For Christians who see it this way, the healing work of doctors, nurses and every careful hand, which they count as God's work too.

orig.note: Greek: physician, healer; the word in "Luke, the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14).

carryVoice: Your line: God heals through hands. Every careful hand counts. That's today, done.
